# Fenwick's schedule showed which instruments awaited parts

At Fenwick Instrument Repairs, a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline began in January 2026. Workshop manager Priya Vale describes what the team had to agree first, what the trial did not measure and what Vale would change before adding older jobs.

By Thomas

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Its jobs awaiting parts and its jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets. The workshop's own records of the trial show what staff gained and what was left open.

## Fenwick defined the statuses, Benchline configured them

Before choosing Benchline, the team checked that the software could tell those two statuses apart. The workshop then defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session, while collection arrangements stayed on the telephone.

Asked by Benchline in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

## The trial left repair speed unmeasured

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

The manager approved continued use for new jobs but put off adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale looks back on the choice

Asked in the same interview whether Vale would make the same choice again, and what would change, the manager wrote: 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

Managers weighing a shared schedule can put the question Fenwick had to settle to their own teams: what does ready for work mean at each bench?

arguments.content:
# Source-support comparison: Fenwick Instrument Repairs case draft

Draft: `scratch/write-run.yejzVk/draft.md`
Material: `work/source.md` (brief plus complete source package)
Language: British English (en_GB). Source language is English, so no quotation is translated. There are no translation findings.
Byline ("By Thomas") is from the invocation environment. It is not a finding.

## 1. Claim accounting

Each draft passage is set beside the source passage it rests on, quoted in the source's own words. Then comes a note on what differs.

### Title
- Draft: "Fenwick reports staff could see instruments awaiting parts"
- Source: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, … says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
- Difference: "Fenwick reports" stands for the workshop's own trial summary, so the assertion stays with the workshop. "instruments awaiting parts" is a close rendering of "which instruments were waiting for parts". The draft does not turn the reported experience into a measured result, which fits "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement". I cannot name a case in which one statement holds and the other fails. Supported.

### Standfirst
- Draft: "At Fenwick Instrument Repairs, a six-week trial of Benchline's shared bench schedule began in January 2026."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." / "Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
- Difference: the source says the trial was of "a shared bench schedule". It never says the schedule tried from January was Benchline's, and it gives no date for choosing Benchline. The draft adds that the schedule was Benchline's from the start of the trial. Concrete case: the team began the trial in January on another shared schedule, then chose and configured Benchline part-way through. In that case the source holds and the draft fails. No supplied statement rules this out. "Benchline configured those choices", "38 jobs entered in the schedule" and "Would you make the same choice again" all leave the timing open. **Finding F1.**
- Draft: "Here is what the team had to agree first, what the trial summary did not measure and what its manager would change."
- Source: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" / Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." / "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." / "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?"
- Difference: "first" matches "before the schedule was useful". Pronoun "its": third person, singular, non-personal (neuter). Its referent is Fenwick / the team, and the source's "workshop manager" matches that. It carries no natural gender for the manager. Supported.

### Paragraph 1
- Draft: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments."
- Source: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." Identical. Supported.
- Draft: "Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work once appeared on separate paper sheets."
- Source: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
- Difference: "once" stands for "Previously". The time scope is the same. Supported.
- Draft: "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, using statuses the workshop defined itself."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices."
- Difference: "itself" stresses that the workshop, not Benchline, did the defining. The source's split between "The workshop defined" and "Benchline configured" supports that. Reflexive pronoun: third person, singular, non-personal (neuter), referring to the workshop. The draft does not say how many statuses there were. Supported.

### Heading: "Fenwick defined the statuses, Benchline configured them"
- Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices"
- Difference: "configured them" (the statuses) is slightly narrower than "configured those choices" (the definitions plus who updates them). That covers part of what was configured and adds nothing. Pronoun "them": third person, plural, no gender, referring to the statuses. Supported.

### Paragraph 2
- Draft: "Before choosing Benchline, the team checked that it could tell those two statuses apart."
- Source: "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." ("these statuses" refers back to "jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work")
- Difference: the order is kept (check, then choice). "two" matches the two named statuses. Pronoun "it": third person, singular, non-personal, referring to Benchline, as in the source. Supported.
- Draft: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
- Source: same words. Supported. "them": third person, plural, referring to the statuses. Same as the source.
- Draft: "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone."
- Source: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."
- Difference: the passive drops the agent ("the team"), but the actor is not changed. "still" stands for "continued". Neither statement says telephone was the only channel. Supported.

### Paragraph 3 (quotation)
- Draft: "Asked by Benchline's case writer, by email on 2 March 2026, what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'"
- Source: "The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale." / Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" / Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench."
- Difference: the quotation is word for word, including the hedge "not always". The question is paraphrased accurately. "replied" fits a written email answer, and no spoken exchange is suggested. Pronouns inside the quotation ("We", "it") are Vale's own. "We" is first person plural (the team including Vale). "it" is third person singular, non-personal (the part). No pronoun anywhere in the draft gives Vale a natural gender. Supported.

### Heading: "The summary leaves repair speed unmeasured"
- Source: "It does not measure repair duration" / "not a measured improvement in repair speed"
- Difference: "repair speed" is the source's own term for the same quantity. Supported.

### Paragraph 4
- Draft: "The workshop's trial summary of 23 February 2026 records 38 jobs in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
- Source: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
- Difference: the draft drops "entered", with no change of meaning. The count is given without any evaluation. Pronoun "It": third person, singular, non-personal, referring to the summary. Supported.

### Paragraph 5
- Draft: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
- Source: same words. Supported. "its": third person, singular, non-personal (the team).

### Heading: "Vale looks back on the trial"
- Source: Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?"
- Difference: this describes the answer that follows. It adds no fact. No pronoun. Supported.

### Paragraph 6 (quotation)
- Draft: "Asked in the same exchange, 'Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?', Vale wrote: 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'"
- Source: Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" / Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
- Difference: the question and the answer are word for word. Both come from the same email interview, as the source says ("a complete extract from an email interview"). "wrote" is accurate. The scope "for new jobs" is kept. "I" is first person singular (Vale). "it" is third person singular, non-personal. Supported.

### Paragraph 7 (closing)
- Draft: "Other managers can put the question Fenwick had to settle to their own teams: what does ready for work mean?"
- Source: Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." / "…not … a recommendation for every workshop."
- Difference: this is the author's own suggestion, and it rests on the supported fact that Fenwick had to settle the question. It does not attribute a recommendation to Vale or Fenwick. It does not recommend Benchline or claim a result for other workshops, so it respects the source's limit. "their": third person, plural, no gender (other managers). Author's advocacy resting on supported material. Not a finding.

## 2. Findings

### Source-support findings

**F1: Standfirst says the trial was of Benchline's schedule from January (low severity)**
- Draft: "a six-week trial of Benchline's shared bench schedule began in January 2026."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." (no date or order given relative to the start of the trial)
- What changed: the draft makes the product the trial used, from its start, a matter of fact. The source names only "a shared bench schedule" for the trial and gives no time for the Benchline choice.
- Case: the trial began in January on another shared schedule, and Benchline was chosen and configured later in the six weeks. The source holds and the draft fails. No supplied statement excludes this.
- Smallest supported repair: "At Fenwick Instrument Repairs, a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule began in January 2026." The body already names Benchline correctly, in "Before choosing Benchline, …".

### Translation findings

None. Source and target are both English, and no quotation is translated.

## 3. Completion status

Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body and closing has been accounted for, and so has every pronoun. There is one source-support finding, F1 (low severity), and it is not fixed in the draft. There are no translation findings.

> Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.
>
> What may be repaired: The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make. That is the whole list.

# Source-support report: Fenwick Instrument Repairs draft

Draft: `draft.md`. Material: `source.md`. Language: en_GB; source is English, so no translation findings arise. The byline ("By Thomas") is out of scope, as stated in the instructions.

## 1. Claim accounting

| # | Draft passage | Source passage (verbatim) | What differs | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | Title: "Fenwick's schedule showed which instruments awaited parts" | "The workshop's trial summary ... It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience" | The source attributes this to the summary ("It says"). The title states it as a fact about the schedule and gives no attribution. | **Finding F1** |
| S1 | "a six-week trial of Benchline's shared bench schedule began in January 2026" | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline" | Nothing material | Supported |
| S2 | "what the team had to agree first" | Q: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." | "First" matches "before the schedule was useful" | Supported |
| S3 | "what the trial left unmeasured" | "It [the trial summary] does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." | The source says the summary does not measure these. The draft says the trial left them unmeasured. | **Finding F2** |
| S4 | "what its manager would change" | Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." | Nothing material | Supported |
| B1 | "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." | Identical sentence | None | Supported |
| B2 | "Jobs awaiting parts once appeared on one paper sheet, jobs ready for work on another." | "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets." | Number: the draft says one sheet for each status. The source says only "separate paper sheets". | **Finding F3** |
| B3 | "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule" | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." | None | Supported |
| B4 | "..., on terms the workshop set itself." | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices" | Scope: "terms" of the trial is wider than status definitions and update responsibility | **Finding F4** |
| H1 | Heading: "Fenwick defined the statuses, Benchline configured them" | "The workshop defined the statuses ... Benchline configured those choices" | "Them" (the statuses) is narrower than "those choices", which also cover who updates, but it stays inside them | Supported |
| B5 | "Before choosing Benchline, the team checked that it could tell those two statuses apart." | "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." | Nothing material. "Two" matches the two statuses named in the previous sentence of the source. | Supported |
| B6 | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session." | Identical in substance | None | Supported |
| B7 | "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone." | "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers." | The passive voice drops "the team" as agent but asserts no other agent. "Still" = "continued". Neither sentence says the telephone was the only channel. | Supported |
| B8 | "Asked by Benchline's case writer, by email on 2 March 2026, what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'" | "email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale" / Q: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" / Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench." | The quotation is verbatim, written (email) and approved. The question is paraphrased faithfully. | Supported |
| H2 | Heading: "The trial left repair speed unmeasured" | "It [the summary] does not measure repair duration" / "The summary and interview establish ... not a measured improvement in repair speed" | Subject shifts from the summary to the trial (same issue as S3) | **Finding F2** |
| B9 | "The workshop's trial summary of 23 February 2026 records 38 jobs in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." | "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." | None. The attribution is kept. | Supported |
| B10 | "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." | Identical | None | Supported |
| B11 | "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions." | Identical | None. The source's positioning is kept, and so is its ambiguity about whether the summary records this decision. | Supported |
| H3 | Heading: "Vale looks back on the trial" | Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" | A retrospective question fits "looks back" | Supported |
| B12 | "Asked whether the same choice would stand and what would change, Vale wrote:" | Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" | Subject and modality change: "would you make ... again" / "what would you change" become "would stand" / "what would change" | **Finding F5** |
| B13 | "'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'" | Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." | Verbatim, written and approved | Supported |
| B14 | "Other managers can start with the question Fenwick had to settle: what does ready for work mean at each bench?" | Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench." / "not ... a recommendation for every workshop" | The question attributed to Fenwick adds "at each bench". The advice to other managers is the author's own. | **Finding F6** for the attributed question; the advice itself is covered in Note N1 |

### Pronoun accounting (person, number, natural gender)

- Standfirst: "its manager" is third person singular and neuter, referring to the workshop/team. It asserts no natural gender. Supported.
- B5: "it could tell" is third person singular and neuter, referring to Benchline, as in the source's "it could distinguish". Supported.
- B6: "update them" is third person plural and refers to the statuses, as in the source. H1 "configured them" is also third person plural (the statuses). Supported.
- B10: "It" is third person singular and neuter, referring to the summary, as in the source. Supported.
- B11: "its status definitions" is third person singular and neuter, referring to the team, as in the source. Supported.
- Quotations: "We", "I" and "it" (a part) are Vale's own first-person and neuter forms, copied verbatim. Supported.
- Vale is never given a gendered pronoun in the draft ("Vale replied", "Vale wrote"). The material gives no natural gender for Vale, and the draft asserts none. No finding. The repair to F5 must keep it that way.

## 2. Findings (all source-support; there are no translation findings)

**F1: Title turns a reported statement into an unattributed fact**
- Draft: "Fenwick's schedule showed which instruments awaited parts"
- Source: "It [the trial summary] says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." and "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience".
- Difference: the source says whose statement this is (the summary). The title asserts it as an established fact about what the schedule did.
- Test case (fits the material): the summary says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts, but the schedule sometimes failed to show some of them. For example, a status was left un-updated, which Vale's remark that a part "did not always" reach the right bench makes easy to picture. The source sentence still holds and the title fails. No supplied statement excludes this case.
- Smallest repair: "Fenwick's trial summary: staff could see which instruments awaited parts" (or "Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts, its trial summary says").

**F2: "The trial left ... unmeasured" in place of "the summary does not measure"**
- Draft: the standfirst says "what the trial left unmeasured", and the heading says "The trial left repair speed unmeasured".
- Source: "The workshop's trial summary ... does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." and "The summary and interview establish ... not a measured improvement in repair speed".
- Difference: the subject shifts from the summary document to the trial as a whole. What the summary does not report is thereby presented as known not to have happened during the trial.
- Test case (fits the material): the schedule logged job timestamps and somebody worked out repair durations during the trial, but the summary does not report them. The source holds and the draft fails. No supplied statement excludes this case.
- Smallest repair: standfirst "what the trial summary did not measure"; heading "The trial summary did not measure repair speed".

**F3: "one paper sheet ... another" in place of "separate paper sheets"**
- Draft: "Jobs awaiting parts once appeared on one paper sheet, jobs ready for work on another."
- Source: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
- Difference: number. The draft says there was exactly one sheet for each status. The source says only that the two kinds of job were on separate sheets.
- Test case (fits the material): jobs awaiting parts ran across several sheets, and jobs ready for work were on other sheets. The source holds and the draft fails. Nothing supplied excludes this case.
- Smallest repair: "Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work once appeared on separate paper sheets."

**F4: "on terms the workshop set itself"**
- Draft: "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule, on terms the workshop set itself."
- Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
- Difference: scope. The "terms" of a trial include its length, scope, cost and success criteria. The source only has the workshop defining statuses and deciding who updates them.
- Test case (fits the material): Benchline proposed the six-week period and the trial conditions, while the workshop defined only the statuses and who updated them. The source holds and the draft fails. No supplied statement excludes this case.
- Smallest repair: delete the clause, or replace it with ", using statuses the workshop defined itself".

**F5: The interview question is paraphrased with a different subject and modality**
- Draft: "Asked whether the same choice would stand and what would change, Vale wrote:"
- Source: Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?"
- Difference: "Would you make the same choice again" asks what Vale would do if choosing afresh. "Would the same choice stand" asks whether the existing decision remains in force. "What would you change" asks what Vale would do differently. "What would change" asks what will change, with no agent. As the draft frames it, Vale's answer reads as a statement about the existing decision and future changes, not as hindsight.
- Test case (fits the material): the existing decision stands (continued use was approved), but when choosing afresh Vale would choose differently. Or the backlog timetable will change anyway, whatever Vale would do differently in hindsight. In each case one question and the other get different answers. No supplied statement excludes this case.
- Smallest repair: quote the question and add no gendered pronoun. For example: "Asked, 'Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?', Vale wrote:". Do not use "whether she would ...": the material gives Vale no natural gender.

**F6: The question attributed to Fenwick adds "at each bench"**
- Draft: "... the question Fenwick had to settle: what does ready for work mean at each bench?"
- Source: Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench."
- Difference: scope. Fenwick settled what "ready for work" meant. The draft says it settled what the term means at each bench, which implies a definition for each bench.
- Test case (fits the material): Fenwick agreed one workshop-wide definition, for example "the part has reached the right bench", and did not define it bench by bench. The source holds and the draft's attribution fails. No supplied statement excludes this case.
- Smallest repair: "... the question Fenwick had to settle: what does ready for work mean?" (If the author wants the bench angle, it can be added as the author's own suggestion rather than as Fenwick's question.)

## 3. Notes (not findings)

- **N1 (editorial question):** "Other managers can start with ..." is the author's own advice, resting on supported material, and is worded permissively. It does not attribute a recommendation to Fenwick or Vale, so it does not conflict with "not ... a recommendation for every workshop". The brief says "No ... call to action is supplied". Whether this closing line counts as a call to action is an editorial question for the commissioning party, not a source-support defect.
- The quotations are email text approved by Vale, and both are verbatim. No repair was needed and none was made. The spoken-quotation rules do not apply.
- Hedges and qualifications are kept elsewhere ("says staff could see"; the exclusions for duration, revenue and satisfaction; "postponed ... until"). No causal claims are made.

## 4. Completion status

Complete. All claims in the title, standfirst, headings, body and closing were accounted for. Unresolved findings: F1, F2, F3, F4, F5 and F6 (all source-support; there are no translation findings). N1 is an open editorial question.
